mappings.title: S.F.'s brief heat wave is ending, making way for more foggy weather
mappings.summary_detail: San Francisco is finally showing signs of summer heat as the month draws to a close. Tuesday marked the second consecutive day that parts of the city’s east side reached the low 80s. This briefly narrowed the typical temperature gap with the traditionally warmer interior areas of the East and North Bay, where temperatures peaked in the mid-90s on Tuesday.  But you just need to look toward the ocean to see what’s coming for the city, and eventually for the entire region.  The marine layer has been slowly thickening over the past few days and will be more noticeable Wednesday, especially during morning and evening hours. However, it’s not yet strong enough to dominate the day with clouds. Temperatures will again rise into the upper 70s in the city and into the 80s and 90s across the rest of the Bay Area. Starting Thursday, the atmospheric flow across the region will become less amplified. This shift will allow for more coastal clouds and fog, leading to cooler temperatures across the interior through the weekend.  Wednesday breakdown San Francisco: More low clouds and fog are expected across the city, clearing more slowly, especially on the typically foggy west side. Temperatures will remain warm, reaching the upper 70s downtown and in South of Market. The Mission and Sunset districts will see temperatures in the mid- to upper 60s. Clouds will return in the evening. Overnight, the city will be mostly cloudy with lows in the mid-50s. North Bay: It will be another warm and sunny day across the North Bay. Temperatures will climb into the upper 80s to mid-90s from San Rafael through Petaluma, Napa and Santa Rosa, extending to Vacaville and Fairfield. Coastal areas near Sausalito and Vallejo will see highs in the upper 70s. Overnight conditions will be mostly clear, with lows in the 50s. East Bay: Clouds along the bay-facing parts of the East Bay will lift quickly, giving way to a mostly sunny day across the region. Highs will reach the upper 70s in Richmond and Oakland. Fremont and Hayward will see temperatures in the low to mid-80s. Interior areas will experience another warm day, with highs in the low to mid-90s in Concord, Walnut Creek and Livermore. Overnight conditions will be mostly clear, with lows in the upper 50s to low 60s. Pacific Coast and Peninsula: Clouds will linger along the Pacific Coast, with highs in the upper 60s to around 70 in Pacifica, Half Moon Bay and Daly City. The eastern side of the Peninsula will see another mostly sunny day with highs in the 80s from San Francisco International Airport through Redwood City. Overnight will be partly cloudy, especially at the coast, with lows in the upper 50s to low 60s. Santa Cruz and South Bay: Temperatures are expected to reach the low 90s in Sunnyvale, Santa Clara and San Jose. Santa Cruz will experience persistent morning clouds, with the marine influence keeping highs in the mid- to upper 70s. The hills will be warmer, with highs in the 80s. Overnight will be partly cloudy with lows in the upper 50s to low 60s.

mappings.title: Fire evacuations from some parts of Tahoe could take up to 14 hours, new estimate finds
mappings.summary_detail: For years, Tahoe-area officials have estimated it would take less than four hours to clear out a swath of California communities on the lake’s northwest edge — from Kings Beach to Tahoe City — in the event of a major encroaching wildfire. But a new independent analysis, employing artificial intelligence and a consulting agency specializing in fire emergencies, estimates that it could take nine to 14 hours — or more — to clear the tourist-laden area, as drivers gather on roads that may be jammed or closed. “The possible public safety impact of increased evacuation times is significant,” said Doug Flaherty, a retired battalion chief in the city of Orange and a former San Luis Obispo fire marshal. “Technology has allowed for more accurate analyses. Many assumptions stated in community emergency plans are based on subjective and dated information.” Flaherty, the president of the nonprofit Tahoe Sierra Clean Air Coalition, which commissioned the evacuation study set to be released Tuesday morning, called the new estimates “conservative.” He said the analysis “simulates one or two road closures. The reality is that there will most probably be many more.” The study could intensify an existential debate in Tahoe that has only grown since the pandemic, touching on development rules and Airbnb rentals: Has the famed destination become too overrun with visitors? The new study also found that in the Washoe Tahoe area — primarily Incline Village and Sand Harbor State Park — an evacuation of people in an estimated 13,151 vehicles would take roughly seven to nine hours, depending on road closures. Washoe County, in 2022, estimated it would take a minimum of six hours to evacuate 3,842 vehicles out of Incline Village. In 2021, Tahoe dodged a catastrophe when the Caldor Fire tore through the Highway 50 corridor, threatening much of the Tahoe Basin, destroying more than 1,000 structures and creating gridlock for evacuating residents. Photos emerged of fleeing residents stuck in traffic for hours — one man even pulled out a violin to play as he waited. That fire, as well as other deadly blazes that prompted frustratingly slow evacuations, renewed concerns over Lake Tahoe’s plan for future escapes. The Sierra Nevada jewel presents some unique challenges: The region is a major recreational hub, bringing in 60 million visitors annually with a summer apex coinciding with peak wildfire season. The Tahoe Basin also faces jurisdictional hurdles. The lake and its communities include two states, five counties, federal forest land and a city. This complicates a cohesive, regional plan, critics claim. “There is no more important Tahoe land use question today than this,” said Pamela Tsigdinos, an Incline Village resident who volunteered in the evacuation analysis effort. “How many people can the Tahoe basin safely accommodate and evacuate in a geographically constrained, pine-forested, mountainous area with few exits and tens of millions of visitors, many unfamiliar with the terrain?” An official with the Tahoe Regional Planning Agency said she could not comment on the findings without seeing the methodology and data, but said Tahoe Basin fire chiefs and its police and emergency management agencies were working to coordinate evacuations at a regional level. “In recent community meetings, Tahoe Basin emergency responders emphasized that incidents requiring evacuations are dynamic and when and how to direct people during an evacuation depends on the specific circumstances,” said Kimberly Caringer, deputy director of the agency. “Estimates of how long it would take to evacuate are based on many factors, including the type of incident, location of the ignition, wind direction, weather patterns, moisture conditions, etc.” She pointed to the Caldor Fire and early evacuations of 30,000 residents with no loss of life. Caringer said reducing fuels has been a top priority, with authorities conducting more than 75,000 defensible-space inspections on private property since 2008. The agency received $1.7 million to improve communications and transportation infrastructure during emergencies, she said, and has worked to identify Tahoe’s most vulnerable residents. A Washoe County spokesperson said she could not comment on the new analysis because the county had not seen the data, but acknowledged the six-hour time frame to clear out Incline Village cited by the county relied on “outdated data.” “At the time the plan was written it was accurate, but our community has grown and has more visitors,” spokesperson Bethany Drysdale said. “However, each incident is assessed in the moment by trained first responders responsible for making critical life-safety decisions. Those first responders always err on the side of caution and will evacuate accordingly.” Drysdale said Washoe County Emergency Management was updating its regional evacuation plan, but that the work was “dependent on funding.” “Our funding was cut significantly, which halted our ability to carry out any studies,” she said. Still, she said, the Nevada county has held an evacuation drill in Incline Village and piloted a website to provide real-time updates, among other wildfire preparations. The county hopes to hire a third-party vendor to complete an evacuation study of its most critical areas. Elise Soviar, a Placer County Sheriff’s Office spokesperson, said the agency couldn’t comment on the study without reviewing the findings. “We do not know what data was used by the AI firm to come up with the time estimates,” she said. She said her department holds annual training sessions in the Tahoe Basin with police agencies and fire districts to coordinate wildfire response and evacuations in the North Tahoe region. The analysis was completed by the consulting group PyroAnalysis and AI disaster modelers from Ladris Technologies, who said they conducted more than 400 evacuation simulations, testing out highway and feeder-road limitations and possible road closures that could create choke points. In addition, the models take into account factors including variances in alert systems, evacuee behavior, cell tower reliability, loss of power, evacuations of hikers and cyclists, challenges with vulnerable populations, and social media misinformation. The models focused on a “no-notice” evacuation, an event caused by a wildfire with immediate threat to human life and one that has historically overwhelmed emergency officials and infrastructure. The consultants plan to finish additional studies next month on Douglas Tahoe, El Dorado South Shore Tahoe (including Meyers and Fallen Leaf Lake) and El Dorado West Shore. The Placer County model estimates a nine to 14-plus-hour evacuation time depending on road closures. The group estimated that 17,577 vehicles would flee the area, taking nine hours if Highway 89 was shut down northbound, and up to 14 hours if Highway 28 eastbound and Highway 267 northbound were shut down. The last evacuation estimate for this part of Placer County came in the county’s 2016 California Environmental Impact Statement, which estimated 3.7 hours. In the 2017 Placer County Tahoe Basin Area Plan, the agency acknowledged that emergency evacuation would overwhelm roadway capacities “under any scenario and at any hour.” With all roads open in the Incline Village area, the new study predicts a seven-hour evacuation of 13,151 vehicles. However, with simulations of road closures at one specific spot — either state Route 28 at Stateline, state Route 431 at Fairview, or state Route 28 at Sand Harbor — the estimate rises to around nine hours. Residents and stakeholders have been clamoring for a new comprehensive evacuation study for years. Last year, seven retired firefighters wrote a letter to Placer County supervisors opposing changes to the Tahoe general plan for that county that would increase allowable building density and heights, among other changes. They recommended an “evaluation of potential significant impacts in population safety, under a variety of potential wildfire behavior scenarios.” They warned that previous studies failed to look at possible choke points during a sudden surge, and that panicked visitors unfamiliar with the area might turn around due to heavy traffic and flee into the cold lake waters — similar to last year’s Lahaina tragedy in Maui. Flaherty said that, for years, government entities tasked with evacuation planning had used “subjective and dated” time estimates to push forward new development. “From a life safety standpoint this is dangerous, irresponsible and not sustainable,” he said. Caringer, with Tahoe’s regional planning agency, said lower estimated evacuation times do not in fact allow for more development, adding that the Tahoe Basin is “approaching buildout.”

mappings.title: Bay Area tech layoffs: Apple announces rare wave of job cuts
mappings.summary_detail: Apple has implemented a rare wave of layoffs, affecting about 100 positions within its services group.  The impacted employees at the Cupertino-based tech giant were informed of the cuts on Tuesday, Bloomberg reported. The layoffs spanned various teams under Senior Vice President Eddy Cue. The job cuts include roles primarily associated with the Apple Books app and Apple Bookstore, as the company shifts its focus to other divisions.  Additionally, other services teams, such as the one managing Apple News, also experienced layoffs. While Apple has largely avoided mass layoffs even as other major tech companies have downsized, it did lay off 614 employees in Santa Clara earlier this year.  Those cuts marked Apple’s first significant job reductions since the onset of the COVID-19 pandemic and coincided with the cancellation of its decade-long electric car project. Earlier this month, Apple held its third-quarter earnings call, revealing $85.8 billion in revenue, surpassing estimates.  Despite a slowdown in iPhone sales, services flourished, and the newly launched iPad lineup pushed its revenue up by 24% year-over-year. Apple CEO Tim Cook expressed optimism about the upcoming launch of Apple Intelligence, with the rollout expected to begin later this year. The company also announced that, in a planned transition, Chief Financial Officer Luca Maestri will step down on Jan. 1 but will remain involved in corporate services.  Kevan Parekh, vice president of financial planning and analysis, will succeed Maestri as CFO and join the executive team.

mappings.title: Court orders hearing on potential racial bias in South Bay murder verdict
mappings.summary_detail: At Jermaine Howard’s murder trial for a fatal shooting in San Jose, the prosecutor repeatedly asked the Black defendant about his childhood in East Palo Alto, a community known for its minority population and reputation for violence. That was enough, a state appeals court ruled Tuesday, to support a claim of potential bias under California’s Racial Justice Act.“Courts have recognized that a person’s place of residence may serve as a proxy for race,” said the 6th District Court of Appeal.The court did not say Howard’s trial had been affected by racism, but ordered a Santa Clara County Superior Court judge to hold a hearing where both sides could present evidence on the issue. If the judge finds that the verdict may have been influenced by racial bias — whether intentional or not — Howard would be entitled to a new trial.Howard, who owned a food truck business in San Jose, fatally shot an Oakland man identified by the court as Reinol H.M. at a San Jose nightclub in February 2021. Howard testified that he was afraid of Reinol, who was armed, and shot him in self-defense, but a jury convicted him of second-degree murder, and he was sentenced to 19 years to life in prison.The Racial Justice Act, which took effect in 2021, goes further than previous state or federal laws by invalidating convictions that were influenced by racial bias or discriminatory language used by anyone in the case — the judge, lawyers for either side, an expert witness or a juror — even if the bias was unintentional or unconscious.Another state appeals court upheld the law last October, saying the Legislature had the power to set new and more demanding standards for bias-free trials. The state Supreme Court denied review and left the ruling intact.Howard’s jury was obviously aware of his race as he sat in the witness box. The question before the court was whether the conduct of the trial, and particularly the prosecutor’s cross-examination of Howard, called undue attention to his race, or implied that it was a cause of the murder, in a way that could have appealed to prejudice among any of the jurors.After Howard testified that he was raised “between Menlo Park and San Jose,” the prosecutor asked him several times about his upbringing in East Palo Alto. African-Americans were once the city’s largest racial or ethnic group, but Latinos make up about two-thirds of the current population of 30,000.The subject had not been raised by any other witnesses at the trial, and after the verdict, Howard’s lawyer accused the prosecution of trying to bias the jury. In addition to its minority population, attorney Joseph Doyle said in a court filing, “East Palo Alto has a reputation for being unsafe, violent, gang-related, and other negative connotations.”The district attorney’s office replied that the evidence was relevant to Howard’s identification, and Superior Court Judge Robert Hawk found no reason to believe the trial had been affected by racial bias. The appeals court agreed Tuesday that the prosecutor’s questioning was relevant to Howard’s identity and credibility, but said it may also have been an appeal, intentionally or not, to racial bias. In view of “East Palo Alto’s historical reputation and demographics, and the recognized connection between a person’s place of residence, racial group, and negative stereotypes, we conclude that Howard produced facts that, if true, establish that there is. . . more than a mere possibility that the prosecutor used racially discriminatory language. . . or otherwise exhibited racial bias,” Justice Allison Danner wrote in the 3-0 ruling.  Another issue involved the racial slur known as the “n-word.” During closing arguments, the prosecutor told jurors that Reinol’s use of that word before Howard shot him was “not offensive in Mr. Howard’s world.” The appeals court said it would not decide whether the prosecutor’s reference to the word could have been an appeal to racism, because Howard’s lawyer did not raise the issue before Judge Hawk. But Danner said the defense could add the argument to its case when it returns to Hawk’s court. Asked about the ruling, Sean Webby, spokesperson for Santa Clara County District Attorney Jeff Rosen, said, “we are reviewing the decision.” Doyle, Howard’s lawyer, could not be reached for comment.

mappings.title: Sonoma County man who tortured, abused adoptive children sentenced to life in prison
mappings.summary_detail: A Sonoma County man who tortured his three adoptive children for years while collecting state adoption assistance benefits was sentenced Tuesday to life in prison without the possibility of parole, according to the Sonoma County District Attorney’s Office.Jose Centeno, 57, of Rohnert Park was found guilty by a July jury of three counts of kidnapping for financial gain, three counts of torture and nine counts involving the sexual abuse of a child. He was sentenced Tuesday to six consecutive sentences of life in prison without the possibility of parole, three consecutive life sentences, and an additional 39 years in the California Department of Corrections and Rehabilitation.In 2006, Jose and Gina Centeno adopted three siblings ages 2, 3 and 4 years old and enrolled them at John Reed Elementary School. In 2010, after a school staff member filed a report to Child Protective Services on suspicion of physical abuse, the Centenos pulled the children out of school and hid them in captivity.The Centenos told neighbors and extended family that the children had been given back to the state and were not living in their home. In reality, the Centenos confined the three children in an upstairs bedroom with a boarded-up window and chained them to their beds. At one point, the oldest sibling, Kaya, lost consciousness from the abuse. Her siblings were told that Kaya had been sent away, and they never saw or heard from her again. For years, one of the remaining siblings was not allowed to leave the upstairs bedroom except when Jose Centeno would take her to another room and sexually abuse her. In late 2018 or early 2019, Jose Centeno took the two younger siblings to live with family members in Mexico.All the while, the Centenos told state officials that the children were still in their care and received hundreds of dollars each month through the Adoption Assistance Program. They collected these benefits until their crimes were discovered in 2020.After the two younger siblings told people in Mexico about their abuse, Mexico CPS in July 2020 alerted Sonoma County CPS, kicking off a criminal investigation.Jose and Gina Centeno were arrested in August 2020. Gina Centeno was charged as well but died before the trial commenced. Sonoma County Superior Court Judge Troye Shaffer sentenced Jose Centeno to the maximum potential sentence for his charges. The oldest sibling, Kaya, still has not been found. Based on witness statements, she is believed to have disappeared in 2012, when she was 10 years old. “While appropriate that Mr. Centeno will be spending the rest of his life in prison, our two brave victims are still missing their sister Kaya,” said District Attorney Carla Rodriguez. “Though justice has absolutely been served in this case, Kaya will always be in our thoughts.”Anyone with information on Kaya’s whereabouts is asked to contact the Rohnert Park Department of Public Safety at 707-584-2630. Her missing person page can be found on the website of the National Center for Missing & Exploited Children.

mappings.title: Free naloxone vending machines added in Marin County
mappings.summary_detail: Vending machines that dispense free naloxone, a nasal spray that can reverse the effects of opioid overdoses, have been installed throughout Marin County, public health officials announced Tuesday. The installation comes ahead of International Overdose Awareness Day on Saturday, and it’s part of the county’s effort to reduce opioid overdoses, the county’s leading cause of death in residents 55 and under, according to a news release. Marin County now has eight naloxone vending machines and three Naloxboxes, wall-mounted boxes containing naloxone doses, according to an interactive map of naloxone distribution sites available online.“We’re excited to expand the availability of naloxone throughout the county,” said Dr. Todd Schirmer, director of behavioral health and recovery services for the county of Marin. “The new interactive map on the OD Free Marin website allows everyone to do their part by locating and carrying naloxone so they can be prepared for emergencies.”Though naloxone is available for purchase over the counter or by prescription, the new vending machines are an effort to expand access to people without insurance or who cannot afford the medication, officials said.“Vending machines are a great way to make sure everyone has access to Narcan in a no-questions asked, cost-free and equitable way,” said Dr. Matt Willis, Marin County public health officer, referring to a brand name for naloxone.OD Free Marin, a community-based overdose prevention coalition, will teach residents how to use naloxone to save a life at a Saturday event.Other Bay Area counties have also worked to make naloxone more available. San Mateo County officials in May installed a naloxone vending machine in the lobby of Redwood City’s Maguire Correctional Facility.According to the California Department of Public Health, people who use drugs, people who take high-dose opioid medications prescribed by a doctor, and the family and friends of people at risk of opioid overdoses should carry naloxone on their person and at home.

mappings.title: No foul play suspected in Burning Man 2024 attendee’s death, officials say
mappings.summary_detail: No foul play is suspected in the death of an attendee at the 2024 Burning Man festival in Nevada’s Black Rock Desert, authorities have reportedly confirmed. Kendra Frazer, 39, was found unresponsive on Sunday at 11:30 a.m. Her place of residence was not disclosed. Pershing County Sheriff’s Sgt. Nathan Carmichael told the Reno Gazette Journal on Tuesday that the investigation is continuing, but foul play had been ruled out.The investigation is being led by Pershing County Sheriff Jerry Allen, whose jurisdiction is about 45 miles from the festival site, with the Washoe County medical examiner conducting an autopsy. The cause of death may take months to determine.The Regional Emergency Medical Services Authority informed the Reno Gazette Journal that five individuals have been airlifted from the festival due to medical emergencies in the past three days, including a cardiac incident, burns and head trauma.There have been several arrests for charges ranging from aggravated assault to narcotics possession, according to the Pershing County Law Enforcement Association. Burning Man’s policy strictly prohibits illegal substances, including marijuana, at Black Rock City, the temporary city hosting the festival.Law enforcement at the event is overseen jointly by the Pershing County Sheriff’s Office and the federal U.S. Bureau of Land Management. Despite criticisms from Lawyers for Burners, an advocacy group for attendees, who describe law enforcement at the festival as “out of control,” officials expect around 70,000 people at Black Rock City this year, down from 74,000 in 2023 and 75,000 in 2022. This year marks the first time since 2011 that the festival did not sell out.Burning Man will continue through Monday.

mappings.title: This Bay Area surfing town is struggling to house its workers. A co-op could help
mappings.summary_detail: A row of 27 white RVs parked on a dusty parcel off a dirt road is hardly the laid-back sun-kissed surf town vibe that people associate with the West Marin town of Bolinas.But for locals who understand how the town works — its culture, its economy, its schools — what happens with those RVs and the people who live in them has as much to do with the town’s well-being as the historic downtown’s saloon and hardware store, or the tidal estuary that makes up the Bolinas lagoon.Since last October, roughly 60 people, including 18 children, have lived in the RV park on the Tacherra Ranch, a working family farm on Mesa Road that has provided meat, vegetables and eggs to the Bolinas community for over 100 years. Mostly laborers — on ranches, restaurants, construction sites, landscaping crews — they make up just 4% of the town’s population, but their children account for nearly 20% of the tiny K-8 Bolinas-Stinson Union School District.The RV park, which is being managed by the Bolinas Community Land Trust, is a temporary layover on a crusade to create a permanent home for that group of local workers. The land trust is working with Habitat for Humanity and the residents to design and raise money needed to build a housing co-op for the families. The 27-unit project, which the families would help build with Habitat for Humanity staff and volunteers, would be next to the RVs on the Tacherra Ranch.The saga that led to the RV park, recently named Bo-Linda Vista, is a familiar tale to those who follow the poor living conditions endured by agriculture workers along the expansive Northern California coast. The issue made headlines in 2023 when a disgruntled employee shot and killed seven workers on two mushroom farms in Half Moon Bay. After the shooting, Gov. Gavin Newsom toured several farms, calling attention to what he said were deplorable living conditions, without running water or heat.Bolinas, population 1,280, is a place where every third car seems to have a surfboard strapped to the roof, where packs of kids bike down the cottage-lined dusty street that ends at the beach, where the Gospel Flat Farmstand runs on the honor system and features hand-drawn signs that say things like “We Need Your Berry Baskets.”Yet, under the laid-back surface is an economic reality that the people who work most of the jobs in the town can’t afford the $3,500 rents for a two-bedroom apartment or $1.7 million to buy a three-bedroom house. Annie O’Connor, executive director of the land trust, calls the plan to build a 27-unit co-op for the workers a “preservation project” aimed at protecting the economic and cultural diversity that allows isolated coastal towns like Bolinas to remain self-sufficient. “We have a relatively small school and the youth that live at Bo-Linda Vista make up an important percentage of every class,” O’Connor said. “They are an essential and vital part of our community. Their parents work on local ranches and farms. They help keep house, take care of children, care for elders, they supplement that work with service industry, restaurants and short-term rentals and small hotels.”For decades the immigrant families now living at the RV park stayed in a collection of trailers and sheds on the edge of the Tacherra Ranch. Drinking water came from garden hoses and there was no heat or toilets other than portable toilets.The Tacherra family has been criticized for allowing conditions to deteriorate as much as they did. On the other hand, the ranchers were the only Bolinas property owners who gave the community of workers a place to stay, as rough as it was.“They got in over their head as far as the housing they were providing,” O’Connor said.“What started off with good intent ended up having a negative impact.”Eventually, in 2022, the county condemned the property, forcing the land trust and the county to scramble to create the temporary RV park while working on a permanent affordable housing development.Magdelano Garcia, a house cleaner who is living in one of the RVs with her husband and three children, came to Bolinas to join her father, who worked at Star Route Farms.“There were space issues and cleanliness issues but they accepted us on the ranch,” she said. “We got to know Jim (Tacherra) and he worked with our family to improve drastically the conditions, but toward the end the trailers were deteriorating.”Magdelano said the RVs are more cramped than the trailers the family had lived in, but the trade-off is worth it if they can be part of a permanent co-op.“After the county red-tagged the ranch we didn’t know where we were going to go,” she said. “We are really hopeful that we will be able to continue to live in Bolinas and be a part of the permanent housing project.”But while the project has the support of elected officials, county bureaucrats and the vast majority of residents, a group of neighbors calling itself Bolinas for Compassionate Land Use appealed the decision to establish the RV park to the California Coastal Commission, arguing that the temporary use is unrelated to the agricultural or recreational use of the parcel and that it violates the 1965 Williamson Act, which protects farm and ranch land. The group also claims the RV park will negatively impact nearby wetlands and violates a Marin County law that doesn’t allow camping for more than 30 days.“The project’s rushed processing has resulted in a poorly planned development that neither protects the environment, nor provides sustainable, quality, and lawful affordable housing for the Tacherra Ranch tenants,” the appeal states.The Coastal Commission is set to decide whether to hear the case at an October meeting, although commission staff has already determined that the appeal should not be taken up. The staff report said that the RV park would not impact wetlands and that removal of the red-tagged substandard housing and septic/sewage apparatus would lead to a net environmental benefit. “There is a little NIMBY opposition but it represents a very small group of people,” said Jack Seidman, attorney for the Tacherra family and a longtime Bolinas resident. “They argue the RVs are disturbing some pristine natural wetland. It’s a bunch of baloney. This was a huge chicken yard before.”The red-tagging of the property and the legal skirmish headed to the Coastal Commission is only the latest chapter in drama that has played out at the Tacherra Ranch. A 14-year-long legal dispute between brothers Ernest and James Techerra resulted in Marin Superior Court appointing a receiver to take over the property and sell it in order to pay existing debts and obligations. The land trust, which acquired 20 acres of the ranch in 2018, is in contract to buy the remaining 46 acres. Members of the Tacherra family will be part of the new housing co-op and will continue to operate the ranch, which has chicken and cattle and some produce.On a recent Friday, resident and nonprofit leaders met with a group of county officials, including Marin County Administrator Derek Johnson, Supervisor Dennis Rodoni and Marin Community Development Director Sarah Jones. Johnson told the group, “We have to make sure we are addressing substandard housing wherever we can and doing it in a human-centered way.”“These are the people we need to make sure stay here on the coast and that we have a coast that is representative of all demographics and doesn’t just become an exclusive place for those who are wealthy,” Johnson said.Ezequiel “Zeke” Guzman, an organizer who advocates for farmworker and low-income communities, toured the makeshift accommodations before the county condemned the structures. He said the co-op model has worked in the Central Valley.“There were conditions no family should live in. I’ll be honest with you, when I saw what was going on I had a tear in my eye,” Guzman said. “These are the ones who put food on the table and they can’t afford the food that they harvest.”Cassandra Benjamin, interim director of housing for the Marin Community Foundation, said that, if successful, the Bo-Linda model is one that could be replicated elsewhere in the expensive North Bay. “There isn’t affordable housing out here,” Benjamin said. “The only place people can find something for less than $2,000 a month is settings like this, a ranch where the habitability standards are not what they need to be.”The days when private property owners like the Tacherras were on the hook to meet the housing needs of a significant population that drives much of West Marin’s economy are past, she said.“There folks are just not counted. They are in unpermitted housing. They are in jobs that are under the table. And yet our schools would be lost without these kids. They wouldn’t stay open. Our restaurants would not stay open,” Benjamin said. “There has to be a way to improve the quality of life for people who make our lives better.”Ingris Perez Lopez, who is a housekeeper at Smiley’s, the historic saloon and hotel that serves as a de facto community center for the town, urged the officials to stay focused on the permanent housing project.“We don’t want this to be the last time you come here,” Lopez said. “We want your commitment because we live in this town and are committed to working day and night. If we have this opportunity we are not going to let it go. We are going to fight.”

mappings.title: Popular Bay Area music festival is the latest in a series of Calif. festival cancellations
mappings.summary_detail: An annual hip-hop festival and celebration of Oakland slated to take place the first weekend of September has been postponed, the festival announced via Instagram.Oakland-based hip-hop collective Hieroglyphics has put on the free, one-day concert called Hiero Day annually since 2012. This year’s event, which was supposed to take place at Frank Ogawa Plaza, will be postponed until 2025, according to the July 23 post.The cancellation of this year’s Hiero Day is the most recent in a series of California music festival cancellations this year. In mid-April, Skull & Roses, a Grateful Dead-themed tribute celebration in Southern California, was canceled with no refunds (Eventbrite eventually opened a refund window for the event). Two weeks later, Sol Blume, an R&B festival in Sacramento, was postponed until the following year, citing venue conditions. Last month, ticket holders of Sierra Nevada World Music Festival in Mendocino County were told they would be receiving no refunds for the concert that was canceled in June. Even big festivals have been forced to reevaluate ticket sales — earlier this month, Burning Man made an unprecedented move to continue selling tickets less than three weeks before the start of the event. Earlier this year, the Coachella Valley Music and Arts Festival saw its slowest ticket sales in a decade.For Hiero Day, the problem may be financial. The festival’s organizers currently owe $36,130 — plus late fees — to the company hired for stage production and security for last year’s festival, Ungaffable Productions, as reported by the San Francisco Chronicle (The Chronicle and SFGATE are both owned by Hearst but have separate newsrooms).  The Concord-based production group helped put on the 2023 outdoor event honoring hip-hop’s 50th anniversary with three-time Grammy Award-winning rapper Common headlining. The organizers of the event said Oakland contributed fewer dollars in sponsorship than they were promised, but Sean Maher, Oakland’s director of communications, told the Chronicle that the city does not have any additional financial obligations to the festival. In the meantime, Ungaffable Productions owner Tony Garcia said he has had to pay his workers using personal loans and maxed-out credit cards, the outlet reported.“We’re a small business, it’s not like we have millions of dollars to just wash this away,” he told the Chronicle.

mappings.title: Two '90s rock juggernauts play $20 Bay Area show
mappings.summary: Plus, a new Oakland night market and a Japanese collectible craze's landfall in San Francisco
mappings.summary_detail: Summer in San Francisco can be a bitter affair. While your friends in Oakland and on the peninsula post photos of themselves lounging in the sun, you’re stuck under the same blanket of gray, praying for a ray to pierce through. But dull weather doesn’t have to mean dull living. Sometimes, bright spots are just a bridge away; sometimes, you can throw on a layer and find them right at home. To prove it, we started Fogcutter, a new column where we send SFGATE’s sharpest eyes and ears into the field to report on notable Bay Area moments from the past week, breaking down the wonderful (and occasionally wacky) bits and pieces that make it home. In this edition, we cover a $20 anniversary show for two big-name ’90s bands, New Orleans jazz and the gachapon capsule craze’s new home in San Francisco. Read on to see this week’s highlights. Two 1990s rock juggernauts: $20It was still light when ’90s alt-rockers Live came on Friday at Concord Pavilion, playing a ferocious, hour-plus set against the backdrop of the golden East Bay hills that included hits (“Lightning Crashes,” “I Alone,” “All Over You”) and less commercial songs, such as “The River.” By the time the next band, Stone Temple Pilots, was in full swing, it was dark and my Generation X heart was full. It was the kick-off to a monthlong tour celebrating the 30th anniversaries of their career-defining albums — “Throwing Copper” and “Purple,” respectively. Tickets were only $20, and these co-headliners crushed it. Scott Weiland’s voice defines this era for me, and I was worried vocalist Jeff Gutt, who has been with the band since 2017 (Weiland was fired in 2013 and died in 2015), wouldn’t measure up. But he delivered, with rich, guttural, eerily Weiland-esque vocals on all the sonic juggernauts: “Vasoline,” “Interstate Love Song,” “Big Empty” and “Meatplow.” The band played “Purple” in its entirety — the first time ever with Gutt — and guitarist Dean DeLeo, who played masterfully, just as I remember him doing at a San Diego show in 1996, thanked us for the opportunity.,

mappings.title: ABC7 proud new home of San Francisco Chinese New Year Parade
mappings.summary: Mark your calendars and watch the 2025 San Francisco Chinese New Year Parade live on ABC7, Saturday, February 15, 2025!
mappings.summary_detail: SAN FRANCISCO (KGO) -- Mark your calendars, the largest Lunar New Year Celebration outside of Asia is coming to ABC7 this February. ABC7 is now the official broadcast partner of the San Francisco Chinese New Year Parade.Read the full press release here.ABC7 is home to the largest parades in the Bay Area and is proud to now be the exclusive media partner of the San Francisco Chinese New Year Parade."ABC7 Presents: The San Francisco Chinese New Year Parade" will be available to all audiences live, Saturday, Feb. 15, 2025 wherever you stream ABC7.Lunar New Year begins January 29, 2025.

mappings.title: Woman, 47, and boy, 14, killed in wrong-way collision on Bay Area highway
mappings.summary_detail: A 47-year-old woman and a 14-year-old boy were killed when a man drove in the wrong direction on a Bay Area freeway in the middle of the day on Monday, officials said.The California Highway Patrol said in a news release that they received a report at 3:40 p.m. of a wrong-way driver traveling south in the northbound lanes of state Route 85 near Saratoga Avenue in the South Bay. The driver was in a white Toyota Tacoma and speeding, CHP said.As CHP officers were responding, the driver of the Toyota hit a white Tesla Model Y head-on in the northbound lanes of state Route 85 south of state Route 87, CHP said.The Tesla driver and the teenage passenger, both from San Jose, died. The Toyota driver, a 39-year-old man from Orlando, Florida, was taken to a hospital with “major injuries,” CHP said.Northbound 85 in the area of the collision was temporarily closed while investigators collected evidence. The collision remains under investigation. CHP said that it’s not known whether the truck driver was driving under the influence. The Tesla driver and the teenage passenger, both from San Jose, died. mappings.title: Stern Grove Festival sues the city of San Francisco over massive flood
mappings.summary: The lawsuit asks for more than $335,000 in damages regarding the 2021 flood of the park
mappings.summary_detail: A massive flood that covered a venue in mud and canceled a concert three years ago has pitted San Francisco’s oldest outdoor music series against the city, spilling over into a lawsuit filed Friday. The Stern Grove Festival Association, which has been hosting free, open-air concerts in the city park of the same name since 1932, sued the city on Friday, demanding more than $335,000 in damages after a 2021 water main break flooded the historic venue. Bob Fiedler, the executive director of the association, said in an email to SFGATE that the city “has worked hard” to clean up the grove but the nonprofit organization is still seeking more financial reimbursement.“This complaint was filed merely as a procedural necessity, as we work on an amicable resolution with the City to recover some reimbursement of lost revenue and expenses to the Festival,” Fiedler said.The August 2021 flood sent 700,000 gallons of water into the park, which features a sunken natural amphitheater that sits below street level. The water brought a “landslide of water and debris” into Stern Grove, damaging the concert meadow as well as the buildings and bathrooms used by the association, according to Friday’s lawsuit. Matthew Goldman, the chairman of the festival, told SFGATE in 2021 that the flood rendered “our concert meadow completely destroyed.” The water main break occurred near Sloat Boulevard and 22nd Avenue during maintenance on a transmission line after a valve failed, according to a report from the San Francisco Public Utilities Commission. Crews then kept the pipeline open while they worked to reroute water in order to “maintain water service to customers throughout western San Francisco,” according to a 2022 report. The resulting flood heavily eroded the slope leading down to Stern Grove, damaging tennis courts, bathrooms and requiring the removal of 63 large eucalyptus trees. The city then spent $23 million removing debris, restoring buildings and stabilizing the damaged hillside, according to the SFPUC.The flood came just days before the final show of the 2021 Stern Grove concert series, a planned performance with Tower of Power and Too Short. The association then had to cancel the event, which the organization said would have been their most profitable concert of the year (it was rescheduled as the 2022 season opener). The association said in Friday’s lawsuit that it “suffered significant financial harm” from the flood and subsequent cleanup.Nancy Hayden Crowley, an SFPUC spokesperson, said in an email to SFGATE that the commission “completed repairs at Stern Grove” and referred all questions to the city attorney’s office. A spokesperson for the city attorney told the San Francisco Chronicle that they’re actively speaking with the association and hope to settle the case without any litigation. (The Chronicle and SFGATE are both owned by Hearst but have separate newsrooms.) The city attorney’s office did not return SFGATE’s request for comment.

mappings.title: Artists at Hunters Point shipyard plead for a new roof
mappings.summary: These Bay Area artists have been waiting years for a solution
mappings.summary_detail: At the Hunters Point shipyard, outside former Navy building 116, San Francisco Bay glitters just offshore on a sunny August day. But inside the aging structure, plastic buckets are grouped at its seams, ready to catch the water that regularly seeps through the roof when it rains. The 27 artists who work inside seem to barely notice the crumbling ceiling anymore, adding an extra bucket when water from a new leak trickles in and spending their limited funds on roof patching when they can. It’s easy for them to let the problem fade into the background when they also haven’t had running water or heat in their studios for more than 15 years. The ongoing maintenance issues might be cause enough to give up on the space for good. After all, the collective of artists remaining in three of the Navy buildings at the shipyard’s “Parcel B” have been promised shiny new construction full of artists’ studios in the future — even if that future was originally scheduled for 2016 and may still be at least four years out. But the irony is that the artists working at these three buildings just want to stay. They love their old, historic Navy warehouses built in the 1940s, with their tall ceilings, big windows and stunning views. And most of all, they love their cheap rents. But after nearly four years of asking for help to fix the roof, they’re at the end of their rope. They don’t think the buildings, which are still owned principally by the Navy and subsequently managed by the city of San Francisco and then by developer Five Point, will survive another winter. From shipyard to artists’ collectiveAfter the Ohlone people were pushed off the fishing land they had occupied for thousands of years, Hunters Point was established as a commercial shipyard in San Francisco around 1870. It operated privately until the U.S. Navy acquired the land in 1940, utilizing the area for building and repairing ships during World War II. The Navy transformed hundreds of acres over the next three decades with dozens of buildings, including housing, and employed thousands of workers. The base was also home to a radiological laboratory after the war, which eventually conducted nuclear decontamination and radiological testing on-site.The Navy shut down operations in 1974, and local businesses were offered space in the buildings. In 1976, sculptor Jacques Terzian saw the potential in the large empty warehouses, renting one as an artist studio, though he admits he didn’t tell his landlord he was an artist at the time, according to a documentary about his contributions to the area. He recruited others, and by 1983, a burgeoning art community had formed at the defunct military site. The group grew to more than 300 artists, one of the largest artists’ colonies in the country, split among a smattering of buildings at the shipyard.It didn’t take long for the artists to have to defend their right to occupy the spaces. The Navy considered reactivating the shipyard in 1985, putting the artists at risk of eviction. After years of protests, the Navy’s plans eventually fizzled, and the shipyard closed for good in 1991. Over the next two decades, new visions for the vast shoreline of southeast San Francisco began to take shape. The idea was for the massive area to be transformed into residential housing, office buildings, parks and open space, even a hotel, much of it spurred by the state’s redevelopment agency in an effort to increase affordable housing. But it all hedged on an environmental cleanup of the Environmental Protection Agency-designated superfund site, led by the Navy, which has been ongoing for more than 30 years at a cost of more than $1 billion. Upon completion of the phased cleanup, each parcel of land would be transferred to the city, which would then turn it over to developer Five Point to begin construction. But just after Five Point broke ground for the new artists’ building on Parcel A in 2018, two employees of Tetra Tech EC, a contractor performing soil radiation testing at the shipyard, pleaded guilty to falsifying results. Construction on the site for the potential artists’ building stopped. The site remained a pile of dirt for three years before it was finally removed, though construction has not restarted. Construction on the housing on Parcel A restarted in 2021 and currently includes the condo and townhome development that boasts “cheap” prices but few nearby amenities. Just this month, the Navy confirmed another delay in further development at Hunters Point, stemming from new radiological items found at the site last year, one on Parcel B and one on Parcel C. The Navy plans to retest the entire site worked on by Tetra Tech EC, which would prolong that cleanup by at least 18 months. It’s unclear how long it would take for construction to begin after it’s complete.No heat, no water, leaky roofsOn a Thursday in August at Building 115 on Parcel B, Lorna Kollmeyer is crafting a plaster shield to adorn a private home in San Francisco. Her business, which specializes in plasterwork that gives the city’s Victorian homes their signature look, is the last remaining ornamental plaster shop in San Francisco and one of just a few in the Bay Area. The workshop itself acts almost as an archive of SF architectural history.Kollmeyer can’t imagine working anywhere else — she’s been in Building 115 since 2010, and she was in another shipyard building before that, starting in 1984. Every inch of the space is utilized. She’s grateful for the wide, tall doors that make it easy to get materials inside, plus the small area she has outside for drying her projects. She may have to walk around 100 feet to use the bathroom — in the nearest portable toilet — but she said she’d never be able to afford this amount of space anywhere else. That includes the new building that’s been proposed for the space adjacent to Building 101, which houses two-thirds of the artists at the shipyard, on Parcel A. In 2011, San Francisco’s Office of Community Investment and Infrastructure hired a consultant to assess each artist’s needs and project their rent costs in the new building. Kollmeyer said her allotted total square footage was far less than she utilizes now and the rent would have risen to a rate that’s unsustainable for her San Francisco legacy business. Next door to her workshop is Building 116, where Julian Billotte, an artist and gilder specializing in restoration, works out of a large top-floor studio flooded with natural light. His past clients include the San Francisco Museum of Modern Art, the city of San Francisco, and numerous churches and private entities with elaborate ceilings and decorative surfaces. He’s the master tenant for the building, having inherited the post from his father, a painter who began working at the shipyard in 1984. He rents spaces to the artists in his building and passes that money on to an entity of Five Point, which leases the space to him.Billotte keeps the rent as low as he can following the indefinite lease he signed in 2008, which requires master tenants to perform regular maintenance of the building. He spends the entirety of the meager profits from these leases on that upkeep. As he walks through his building, he points out failing roof panels, the issue he thinks is most pressing, and the areas of his studio where he never leaves anything without a tarp to protect it. He’s been begging OCII, Five Point and whoever else will listen to fix the roof for at least three years, emailing and calling his contacts. SFGATE reviewed emails and letters from Billotte to both OCII and Five Point dating back to November 2021, searching for a solution to the roof issue.This year, he started showing up at OCII meetings, pleading their case as winter inches closer and closer. Meanwhile, artists just keep replacing the buckets. “There’s nowhere for artists to go. The artists we have are happy to be here, even with the pollution, no water,” Billotte said. “There’s low rent; it trumps everything.” The Shipyard Trust for the Arts, which advocates for the artists working at the shipyard, has also tried to appeal to OCII and anyone who will listen, including Rep. Nancy Pelosi. Barbara Ockel, president of the organization, said she’s written Pelosi multiple letters pleading for funds, arguing the roof replacement goes beyond regular maintenance of the building and the master tenants shouldn’t have to cover the full costs. She said trying to get anything done at the shipyard, with the multiple organizations involved in its ownership and management, is a challenge. “We’re going to continue to fight for it,” Ockel said. “It’s untenable for the artists to have to cover their art with plastic when they leave the studio.”What happens nextIn August, the Navy requested a structural assessment from OCII of the buildings, which would inform any decision to help fund the roof replacement. Thor Kaslofsky, executive director of OCII, said that the assessment is being scheduled.He said OCII’s goal is to keep the artists in the buildings for the time being, but maintenance is ultimately the responsibility of the master tenants, per the leases. Kaslofsky acknowledges that once the assessment is completed, the repairs needed will likely be out of budget for the master tenants. He said they’re looking into getting assistance from the Navy and from Five Point to help out with these costs, but they won’t know what’s possible until they’re estimated. There’s always a chance the buildings are deemed not safe to occupy at all, and the artists could be forced out. Kaslofsky said what could happen in that scenario depends on the findings of the assessment. Kaslofsky said they expect the assessment to take place in early to mid-September, and then it will take a few weeks to get the findings. “​​There’s no wavering from our commitment to maintaining [the artists’] tenancy there and keeping them safe and healthy,” he said.Kollmeyer, the plaster artist, doesn’t expect the roof repairs to happen before the winter. “There’s no impetus to do anything for the building. We have been in the Bermuda Triangle of bureaucracy with the Navy, the city and the developer. Everyone just wants to pass the buck and say it’s not our business,” she said. The Navy did not respond to SFGATE’s request for comment as of publication. Ockel, meanwhile, isn’t placing blame but acknowledges that nothing is getting done and the artists may soon be in an even more challenging spot. “We’re not really taking a position as to whose fault it is, but you know, we really need to get these people talking to each other, and that’s what we’ve been trying to do,” Ockel said. “It’s just everything is so slow.”And now, it’s been so long since the original plans to relocate the artists were created, Kollmeyer thinks it’s time everyone took a step back and reexamined. When they were drawn up, the country hadn’t even entered the Great Recession, let alone lived through COVID-19 and plenty of other events that should inform how we look at developable space in a city like San Francisco. She gestures to all the open space surrounding her, including several vacant buildings. “We just want to encourage people to think big for the arts,” she said. “Especially in this time when San Francisco is losing its funk, and losing the essence of what makes San Francisco San Francisco. It’s right here.”

mappings.title: Steve Young is just as exhausted by the 49ers' Brandon Aiyuk saga as you are
mappings.summary_detail: To San Francisco 49ers legend Steve Young, the Brandon Aiyuk saga has been frustrating to witness not because of what either side has done but because it’s shifting the focus away from winning a Super Bowl.The former Niners quarterback made his first weekly KNBR appearance of the NFL season Monday and shared that he wasn’t a fan of how “noisy” the offseason has been. As every fan of the red and gold knows by now, the Niners are without two major pieces of their offense due to contract disputes: Aiyuk, last season’s breakout receiver, and offensive tackle Trent Williams, the best player in the NFL at his position. Both players are seeking extensions; neither has gone through a full training camp or played in any preseason games throughout this process. Young explained that he understands what Williams is doing. He called the situation a “bummer” and said he would have liked for things to have been resolved sooner, but he also said he knows the tackle has a right to “set the market,” or become the highest-paid player at his position, given his career pedigree.The Hall of Famer did not have the same patience for Aiyuk.“But Brandon, because of his youth, and because he’s not going to set the market yet wants to set the market, says ‘I want to be traded’ and then goes through this — I don’t know, I don’t know how to put it,” Young said. “But it was like, bro, if you want to tear up the contract and do something big, then you might want to go the fifth year and go prove it out to make sure that everybody is on board with you setting the market. Or, if you’re going to ask to be traded, then when they make a trade that works for them, you gotta say you’re up for it. You don’t say, ‘Oh no, that doesn’t work for me.’ Because then it was like, ‘Well, what do you want?’”Part of this saga has involved the Niners giving Aiyuk permission to speak with potential trade suitors that would give him the big money contract he so desperately desires. However, those trades fell through in part because Aiyuk rejected teams the Niners would have traded with, saying no to the Patriots and Browns. That being said, the Niners also reportedly rejected trades with teams Aiyuk was interested in, such as the Steelers.Young added that he believes these negotiations have worn down the relationship between the receiver and the team, calling it “stretched” and “strained,” although he clarified the relationship wasn’t “broken.” He also thinks that the Niners have given Aiyuk an offer that’s more than fair.“I think at the end of the day, Brandon is now sitting in front of a contract that’s probably — 49ers have stretched as much as they can,” Young said. “They don’t want to stretch the market. They don’t want to do it. They don’t think it’s the time.”The big problem, according to Young, is that all of this is playing out while seemingly every other NFC team has not only improved this offseason but done so with the intention of taking out the Niners at the top of the conference food chain. “Even the Cardinals got better, theoretically,” he quipped. It’s a stark comparison with San Francisco, which could very well include two guys on its final 53-man roster who won’t play the first week of the season.“This is not what we want to be doing today; I can guarantee you,” said Young, who played in the last Super Bowl the 49ers won.,

mappings.title: Fairly new 49ers stadium to spend $200M on some basic upgrades
mappings.summary_detail: As questions loom over whether the San Francisco 49ers will give their two disgruntled offensive stars the big paydays they’re looking for, the team announced a $200 million spending spree on Levi’s Stadium.While the price tag is roughly equal to a couple of 49ers stars, you’d be hard-pressed to find anyone who would consider these improvements as exciting as, say, Christian McCaffrey and Nick Bosa.The upgrades to Levi’s Stadium, which opened in 2014, are as follows: a revamped Wi-Fi system, cashierless ordering kiosks for concessions, updated furniture and “technology” for luxury suites, a new video board — which the Niners say will be the largest 4K display in the NFL — and some new energy-efficient LED lighting. Oh, and some ticket holders get a buffet when they walk in now.This is all part of the plan to make Levi’s look as nice as possible for 2026, without a doubt the biggest year in the stadium’s history. Not only is the Santa Clara venue tapped to host Super Bowl 60 that year, but it is also slated to host six World Cup matches, including one game in the knockout round, when the tournament comes to North America that summer. The upgrades aren’t dire (the stadium is only a decade old, after all), but they are helpful. Levi’s isn’t the new kid on the block anymore, with five NFL teams opening new stadiums since the Niners’ new home opened.While some may look at this list of upgrades and wonder why it’s mostly the luxury suites that are getting a new touch, they can take solace in the fact that there was no announced plan to address the parking situation outside the stadium. This means that regardless of whether your future experience watching a game is luxurious or lackluster, the notoriously hellish exit of Levi’s should still even things out in the end.
